intro: Every day you are asked to believe things. A post says a food cures headaches. A friend says a rule is unfair. A page says a cow burned down Chicago. Research is the set of habits that lets you check instead of guess: turn a vague topic into a question that can be answered, find sources that have earned trust, take notes that keep other people's words separate from yours, and put what you found together into an idea nobody handed you. Those habits are the difference between repeating and knowing.

Then comes the writing. An essay that works is not longer or fancier than one that does not. It makes a claim a reader could disagree with, supports it with evidence the reader can check, takes the other side seriously, opens with something worth reading and ends with something worth remembering. This unit walks through the kinds of essays high school asks for, analysis, argument, explanation and narrative, and the moves that make each one work, from the first sentence to the last cut.

By the end you will be able to take a question you actually care about, find and judge sources on it, cite them in MLA style without fear, and write an essay that says something true in your own voice. You will also be able to look at a draft that is asleep, yours or a classmate's, and know exactly how to wake it up.
bigQuestion: How does a writer move from what other people have said to something true that is their own?

timeline.t: A topic becomes a research question with limits on who, when and which angle
Keyword searches on the web, then in a library database, turn up eight possible sources
Each source is tested for authority, accuracy, currency and purpose; three survive
Notes are taken as marked quotations, paraphrases and summaries, with page numbers
A source log records every source and a line about its strengths and limits
An annotated bibliography summarizes and judges each source before drafting begins
Sources are grouped by relationship and a claim emerges that none of them states alone
A first draft: introduction ending in the claim, body paragraphs by idea, counterclaim answered
MLA in-text citations are checked against a works cited list
Revision for clarity and concision cuts the draft by a fifth and rebuilds the opening
The final essay, with its early draft and a reflection, goes into the portfolio

words.d: a specific, answerable question that guides a search for evidence
the knowledge, training or position that gives a source the right to be believed on a subject
an original record made by a participant or witness, or an object from the time being studied
a restatement of a source's idea in your own words and sentence structure
combining ideas from several sources to build a new point that none of them states alone
presenting another person's words or ideas as your own without giving credit
a short note in parentheses within the paper that identifies the source of a fact or quotation
the alphabetical list at the end of an MLA paper giving full details for every source cited
a statement a reader could disagree with, which an essay sets out to support
the writer's explanation of what the evidence does and how it supports the claim
the strongest opposing view, stated fairly within an argument
saying what you mean in as few words as the meaning needs

test.q: Which of these is a research question rather than a topic?
choices: Why did Chicago reverse its river in 1900, and did it work?
test.why: It names a specific who, when and what, and it can be answered with evidence.

test.q: A student adds site:.edu to a search. What does that do?
choices: Limits results to college and university sites
test.why: The site: operator restricts results to one kind of web address.

test.q: A source is written by a professional historian but is thirty years old. Which test does it pass strongly and which one needs a second look?
test.why: The historian gives it authority; its age means the researcher should ask what has changed since.

test.q: Which is a primary source for a paper on the 1871 Chicago fire?
choices: A letter written by a survivor in October 1871
test.why: A survivor's letter from the time is an original record; the others study or summarize such records.

test.q: A note keeps the source's sentence shape and swaps three words. What is it?
choices: A copy that will count as plagiarism if used without quotation marks
test.why: A true paraphrase changes both words and structure; a light swap is still the source's sentence.

test.q: What does synthesis require that stacking lacks?
choices: The writer's own idea connecting the sources
test.why: Synthesis arranges sources around a point the writer makes; stacking just lists them.

choices: A historian's estimate that about 300 people died
test.why: A specific estimate from one source is not common knowledge and must be credited.

test.q: Which is the correct MLA in-text citation for page 42 of a book by Smith?
test.why: MLA uses the author's last name and page number with no comma or p.

test.q: Where does a works cited entry for a magazine article place the article's title?
choices: In italics, after the magazine's name
In quotation marks, before the magazine's name
In capital letters at the end
It is left out; only the magazine is named
test.why: Titles of parts go in quotation marks and come before the italicized container.

test.q: What does an annotation add to a citation?
choices: A summary, an evaluation, and the source's job in the project
The full text of the source
test.why: The annotation reports, judges and assigns each source its role.

test.q: Why is "The story is about freedom" a weak claim for literary analysis?
choices: No reader could disagree with it, and it says nothing about how the text works
test.why: A claim must be arguable and must explain how the text creates its meaning.

test.q: In an argument essay, what must a counterclaim be?
choices: A weak version of the other side that is easy to knock down
The strongest opposing view, stated fairly
A quotation from an expert who agrees with the writer
test.why: A fair, strong counterclaim keeps a disagreeing reader's trust.

test.q: Which introduction opening does the unit recommend?
choices: A specific scene or surprising fact tied to the subject
A sentence beginning with Throughout history
A list of the three body paragraphs
test.why: An opening that belongs only to this subject pulls the reader in.

test.q: Which sentence has a clarity problem?
choices: The fire spread fast because the city was built of wood.
Louise hears the news and goes to her room.
The coach told the player that he was late.
Many readers find the ending sad.
test.why: The reader cannot tell whether he refers to the coach or the player.

test.q: A writer cuts "in order to" to "to" and "at this point in time" to "now." What is she revising for?
test.why: Both cuts say the same thing in fewer words, which is concision.

write.prompt: Make a claim: should Illinois high schools require every student to complete a research paper with an annotated bibliography before graduating? Support your claim with evidence from this unit about what research and essay skills do for a reader and a writer, explain your reasoning, and answer the strongest counterclaim fairly.
tips: State your claim in one sentence a reader could disagree with, at the end of a short introduction that opens with something specific.
Use evidence from the unit: what source evaluation prevents, what synthesis produces, what plagiarism costs, what a portfolio shows.
Explain your reasoning: say why each piece of evidence supports the claim, not just that it does.
State the other side's best point, such as time taken from other work or students who struggle with reading, and answer it honestly.
Cut the draft by a tenth before you turn it in, and put the important word at the end of your last sentence.
